content: Indoor navigation systems are canonically decomposed into three working parts: (1) positioning/anchoring (the 'blue dot'), (2) a digital map modelled as a connected graph of corridors, lifts, stairs, rooms and entrances, and (3) a routing engine that picks the best path from distance, step-free needs and live conditions. 'Wayfinding' is the visitor-facing presentation layer over the same system. QR positioning is documented as a point-fix (non-continuous) method: very low cost, no hardware or batteries, easy to relocate/update, with position known only at scan instants. Zapworks' Complete Guide to Indoor Navigation adds that a good indoor route must model multiple floors via stairs/lifts/ramps, doors and restricted areas, dead ends/security checkpoints, walkable vs non-walkable space, and accessibility constraints - all inside a navigable 'navigation mesh'. Cross-checked across three independent vendor/academic sources.
